extracted.intended_audience: editors, proofreaders, compositors, and publishers (academic press)
extracted.subtask_description: A University-of-Chicago Press manual of style covering hyphenation, word-division, footnote and indexing conventions, tabular composition, spacing, and other typographical/house-style rules for preparing scholarly books and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of maker/dealer/occupation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker,' 'dealer,' and other words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman, the poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions: a few short everyday words (e.g., bookmaker, dressmaker). See note referencing related rule 184.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'store' (hyphenation by prefix syllables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'fellow' always hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family-relationship compounds hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' 'sister,' 'daughter,' 'parent,' and 'foster' should be hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, sister-nation, foster-son, daughter-cells, parent-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'great' for degrees of descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great,' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'skin' spacing rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with one-syllable words are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; but: alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'master' hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke. Exception: masterpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'god' as second element
rubrics_metrics.description: 'God' when forming the second element of a compound should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god. Exceptions: godsend, godson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions spelled out use hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect numerator and denominator with a hyphen unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two-thirds, four and five-sevenths, thirty-hundredths; but: thirty-one hundredths. Do not hyphenate in constructions like 'one half of his fortune...'. (See examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hyphen after 'half,' 'quarter,' etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half,' 'quarter,' etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, half-year, half-title, quarter-mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes semi-, demi-, bi-, tri- (no hyphen ordinarily)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi-,' 'demi-,' 'bi-,' 'tri-,' etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, demigurge, biweekly, bipartisan, trimonthly, tricolor. Exceptions: long or unusual formations (semi-centennial) or where clarity requires (demi-relievo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds beginning with 'self-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'self' as the first element are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect. (See cross-reference note 119.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' (one-word vs two-word)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are one word if the number-word contains only one syllable; otherwise printed as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; but fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with '-like' (hyphenation by syllable/proper noun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun are usually one word if the noun is monosyllabic (with exceptions); if the noun is polysyllabic or a proper noun, they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike). Note exceptions for nouns ending in certain letters (see text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles with 'vice', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', 'lieutenant' (hyphens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of titles such as 'vice,' 'ex-,' 'elect,' 'general,' and 'lieutenant' should be connected to the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds beginning with 'by-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'by-' as first element should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation for co-, pre-, re- before same vowel or w/y
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-,' 'pre-,' and 're-' take a hyphen when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, or by w or y; as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter, co-worker, re-yield; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstall, cohabitation, prehistoric, recast (re-read). Exceptions: proper names, long/unusual formations, and where omission would change meaning (pre-Raphaelite; re-cover vs recover). Note botanical practice (cooperate, reenter) referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words that omit the hyphen (today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen in certain closed compounds of common usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: today, tomorrow, tonight, viewpoint, standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles im-, in-, a- (no hyphen usually) vs non- (usually hyphen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative particles 'im-,' 'in-,' and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen; 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples without hyphen: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, illimitable, impersonal, asymmetrical. 'Non-' examples with hyphen: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious, non-ability; but exceptions without hyphen: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonplus, nonsense, noncombatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hyphen with 'quasi-' prefix
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi-' prefixed to a noun or adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-/under- prefixes generally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not typically be followed by a hyphen, except in unusual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, underestimate, undersecretary; but: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin prepositional prefixes (ante/anti/inter/etc.) generally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin prepositions 'ante,' 'anti,' 'inter,' 'intra,' 'post,' 'sub,' and 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antidote, antiseptic (but: anti-imperialistic per 203), international, interstate, intramural (but: intra-atomic), postscript, postgraduate, postprandial, subconscious, submarine, subtile, subway, superfine. Exceptions listed (ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra/infra/pan/supra/ultra usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixes 'extra,' 'infra,' 'pan,' 'supra,' and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, pan-Hellenic, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate omitted common element in series with hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: When compound words occurring together have a common element omitted from all but the last, indicate the omission with a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; note: some writers object to this usage as a Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate incomplete prefix/suffix or syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or suffix as a particle or syllable not complete in itself, and to indicate syllable division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; the German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein; syllable marking di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common everyday hyphenated words
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain everyday compounds should be hyphenated irrespective of above classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: after-years, bas-relief, birth-rate, blood-relations, coat-of-arms, common-sense, cross-examine, cross-reference, cross-section, man-of-war, death-rate, object-lesson, folk-song, page-proof, food-stuff, pay-roll, fountain-head, poor-law, guinea-pig, post-office, horse-power, sea-level, son-in-law, subject-matter, thought-process, title-page, wave-length, well-being, well-nigh, loan-word, sense-perception, will-power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary divisions of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dividing words across lines wherever possible; carry whole words to next line consistent with good spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: prefer whole-word carryover; good spacing is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing on a two-letter syllable; restrictions by word length
rubrics_metrics.description: In wide measures (20 ems or more) avoid dividing on a syllable of two letters if possible; never carry over a syllable of two letters. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: avoid dividing 'on-ly' (4 letters). Good spacing takes precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive lines ending in hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Never allow more than two consecutive lines to terminate in a hyphen if avoidable. The next-to-last line in a paragraph ought not to end in a divided word; the last line in measures of 15 ems and up should contain at least four letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also try to avoid a divided word at the bottom of a right-hand (recto) page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially personal names, unless absolutely necessary. Do not separate the initials of a name, or combinations like a.d., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry initials and abbreviations intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid separating divisional marks from text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid putting a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) at the end of a line; carry it over with the matter to which it pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the mark with the following section in the same line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation rather than derivation; but where compatible with pronunciation and spacing, prefer etymological/derivational division for compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); knowledge split knowl-edge (not know-ledge). Prefer dis-pleasure over displeas-ure; school-master rather than schoolmas-ter. Avoid monstrosities like Passo-ver, diso-bedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division between two consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, division may be made between the consonants; pronunciation determines the place of division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-der, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing lines at soft c, g, y, or j
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c, g, y (or 'j'); escape the division entirely if possible; if not, divide so as to avoid leaving these single letters at line end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pro-cess (not proc-ess), ne-cessary (not nec-essary), pro-geny (not prog-eny). Note: this differs from some dictionary practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel where practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel when practicable; when a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); read-able (not reada-ble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid creating additional hyphens through division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson, not object-les-son; fellow-being, not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken, not pover-ty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as single letters in division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; do not divide it across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people (do not divide as peo-ple), Caesar, building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules for derivatives with accent shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in a consonant, the consonant in divisions should be carried into next line with the suffix if the accent has shifted; if the derivative retains the accent of the parent word, leave the consonant in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect'); but: respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s adding syllable does not justify new division
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a plural 's' that creates a new syllable for words ending in an 'e' sound does not justify dividing the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid divisions like hor-ses or drounstan-ces (example indicates impossibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division condensed rules (French/German/Italian/Spanish/Greek/Latin)
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing words from commonly encountered foreign languages follow condensed language-specific rules: generally divide on vowels and respect language-specific consonant clusters and compound-word division principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French: divide on vowel; avoid consonant-ending syllables; treat mute e as not forming a syllable. German: divide on vowel where possible; when several consonants between vowels usually carry last to following syllable; treat sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th as inseparable (with exceptions). Italian: divide on vowel; do not separate s before consonant, ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, etc. Spanish: divide on vowel; treat ch, ll, rr as single consonants; follow rules on liquids. Greek/Latin: follow syllable/vowel principles and component-element division for compounds (examples given). See pages for detailed examples in each language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of superior figures and choice of index symbols in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices in running text, use superior figures as a rule. Only in special cases (e.g., tables or algebraic matter where figures would confuse) use asterisks, daggers, etc. Index figures in text should be placed after punctuation marks without space (except in German). When figures are not used, use the symbol sequence: *, †, ‡, §, ||, ¶.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show placement after punctuation; special-case guidance for tabular/algebraic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid., loc. cit., op. cit. in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow closely and uninterruptedly, use 'ibid.' instead of repeating the title; 'ibid.' takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated. 'Ibid.' should generally not be used for the first footnote on a verso page; instead repeat the title if short or use loc. cit./op. cit. where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology ... Ibid. (for subsequent references); guidance on when to use loc. cit. vs op. cit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote formatting for tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables should be set in 6-pt and placed at the foot of the table (not the page). Use asterisks, etc., for reference indices in tables rather than superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instruction to use 6-pt and placement at table foot; exception guidance in 232 for figure use in specific situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit repetition of author's name when in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference or quotation, do not repeat it in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: "I cannot admit..."' — footnote: Laws of the Ancients 1, 153 (no repeat of 'Herbert').

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of index figure in quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is preferable to place the footnote/index figure in the text at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration given in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and abbreviation conventions in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.,' 'chap.,' and 'p.' in references to particular passages; use Roman numerals for Volume, Book, Part, Division (capitals) except classical works which use lower-case roman numerals; use Arabic numerals for number and text pages. Use 'p.' or 'pp.' only when needed to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical references use periods in place of commas for divisions; examples provided for style of English references that may follow classical conventions at author's request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement for periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format shown in illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering conventions for machine-set work
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype-set work, number footnotes consecutively through an article (or chapter in a book) to save resetting; note that some journals (Botanical Gazette, Astrophysical Journal) follow special conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific journal exceptions are listed (e.g., Botanical Gazette numbers footnotes consecutively through an article; others number from 1 on each page unless special cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of Mac/Mc/M', St./Ste. etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: In indexes of proper names, names beginning with Mac, Mc, M', St., Ste. should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte to avoid scattering entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Machiavelli, St. Louis, Maclntyre, etc., given to show placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: hyphenated and compound names
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound and hyphenated names should be listed under the first part of the name; other parts should have cross-references to the primary entry. In cases of hyphenated names gratuitously adopted (e.g., married woman adding maiden name), listing may be under the true name with cross-reference under the preceding element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell-Bannennan, Lloyd-George, Watts-Dunton; 'George, Lloyd-, David. See Lloyd-George.' Guidance on exceptions for adopted hyphenations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names with prefixes (von, de, da, van, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes should generally be listed under the part following the prefix, with noted exceptions by language (English, French with article, Italian/Spanish article-only prefixes, Dutch capitalization, compounded prefixes, and naturalized names treated according to adopted language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hoffman, von; Lima, de; Ponte e Horto, da; English examples: A Backet; De Quincey; Italian/Spanish examples and exceptions listed. When prefix is compounded with the name (Vanderkinde) the prefix letter governs position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlauts and diacritics treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with umlaut (ä, ö, ü) should be listed as if spelled ae, oe, ue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Müller entered as Mueller conventions shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names joined by and/&/y/et/und/e
rubrics_metrics.description: Names or firm names connected by 'and', '&', 'y', 'et', 'und', 'e' should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith & Evans (under 'S'); Gomez y Pineda (under 'G'); Loubet et Meunier (under 'L'). Cross-references guidance: see rule 62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table type and point-size conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: General point-size rules for setting tables depending on the body type size: in 11-pt and 10-pt matter open (unruled) tables ordinarily set in 9-pt leaded; ruled in 8-pt solid. In 9-pt matter both open and ruled set in 8-pt solid. In 8-pt matter open tables set in 6-pt leaded; ruled in 6-pt solid. In 6-pt matter both open and ruled set in 6-pt solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice noted of using different type for totals/averages/percentages; italic and black-face figures may be used to set off classes of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads typography
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with multi-story box-heads, primary heads set in caps and small caps (except where second story consists only of figures); secondary in caps and lower case. The stub head should generally match box-head small-caps usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance covers multi-story box-heads and when figures-only second stories differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rules, spacing, leaders, and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide minimum spacing between rules and table matter, use leaders appropriately, and center/align numbers and text in table columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and matter, and if practicable at least an en quad between vertical rules and matter. In open tables use periods or leaders between columns; in ruled tables use leaders in the stub. For blank numeric cells use leaders across full width; center figures in column; if unequal digits, leave more space on left than right. Reading-matter in columns should be centered; if runover occurs use hanging indention aligned left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rule usage and table style by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double rules at the top of all tables; vertical (perpendicular) rules generally only when a table is doubled up. Tables of two columns should be set as open; three or more as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also guidance on headline typography: 'Table I' set in caps of the table body type; descriptive line in caps and small caps of the same type; single descriptive headline set in caps of the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system and pica standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of typographical measures; the standard of measurement is the pica (12 points = one-sixth inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lines set in 12-pt (pica), 11-pt (small pica), 10-pt (long primer), 9-pt (bourgeois), 8-pt (brevier), 7-pt (minion), 6-pt (nonpareil), 5-pt (pearl). Larger/smaller sizes uncommon in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type styles and manuscript indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and manuscript indications for type styles: roman, italic, and bold face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman indicated by plain; italics indicated in manuscripts by a straight underline; bold face indicated by a wavy line. Examples lines set in roman/italics/bold-face shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of type and font composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology: body of a type is the shank; upper surface bearing character is the face; projecting part is the kern; shank projection is the shoulder. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case; caps indicated by three straight lines, small caps by two in manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of caps, small caps, and lower-case shown for 9-pt roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs linotype spacing systems (units/quads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype uses the unit system (18 units in a quad) with fixed cast spaces; linotype uses the pica system with fixed spaces (em quad, en quad, thin space) and a space band for spreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotype: standard 6-unit space = 3-em space; 5-unit and 4-unit spaces defined, and justification adjusts spaces during setting. Linotype: pica system with em/en/thin spaces; space band spreads spaces between 3-em and slightly larger than an en quad; hand insertion required for spaces smaller than thin space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em, en, and other spaces/dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (em quad) is a block the top of which forms a perfect square (size depends on type); an en quad is half an em; three-em, four-em, five-em, hair-space definitions; dash widths defined by em/en quads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: em dash (—), en dash (-), 2-em and 3-em dashes; examples of lines set with em/en/3-em/4-em/5-em spaces and hair-spacing displayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spacing after punctuation and between words
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard line spacing: a 3-em space between words (not separated by other punctuation) and after commas; an en quad after semicolons and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods and terminal ! or ? concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific sequence and examples provided; see rule 262.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order for reducing/increasing spacing to justify lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When adjusting spacing to justify a line, reduce spacing beginning with commas and slanting letters (large 'shoulder'), and increase spacing beginning with overlapping letters (kerns), straight-up letters, and punctuation other than periods and commas (in that order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical order for spacing adjustments to maintain evenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions for a well-spaced line and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line where most spaces are 3-em, the remaining spaces should be no more than an en quad; this proportion should be maintained when increasing or reducing spacing. To justify a line is to adjust spacing to make it even/true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on avoiding erratic spacing and preserving proportional relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternating very thin and wide spaced lines; forbids hair-spacing to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide one and never hair-space or em-quad a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to preserve even typographic color; do not artificially compress or expand lines with extreme spacing tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last-line spacing and short-word spacing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph to avoid an end indention; short words like 'a' and 'an' should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain visual consistency in word spacing; avoid ragged last-line adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin-space usage with symbols, currency, and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, % and similar signs; before 'f.', 'ff.', and metric symbols. In American and English sums of money no space is used between currency symbols ($, £) and numerals; an en leader may be used for a decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '§ 14. Be it further ordained ...'; 'pp. 10 ff.'; '$2.75; £1035. 2d; 10° C.' (illustrations in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at line beginnings and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of subsections use an en quad; after numerals at start of center-heads use an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise spacing conventions for headings and enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture references and other specialized spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced in the prescribed manner (examples given); between letters forming products and before superior figures or letters indicating powers or indices, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: II Cor. I : 16-20; a : 5 — 3 : 1a; mathematical expressions shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure and point size
rubrics_metrics.description: Indentation measurements vary by measure width and body type: for measures <10 picas indent all sizes 1 em; for 10–20 picas use size-dependent ems (detailed table provided); for 20–30 picas use larger indents (detailed table provided). These guidelines apply to plain paragraphs and hanging indents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed em values given by body size (ii-pt, lo-pt, 9-pt, 8-pt, 6-pt) and measure width; guidance to follow the table for consistent indention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and centering guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let indentation be governed by that line; if the longest line is disproportionate, average the long lines to give a centered appearance. When quotations from different poems follow in succession, indent alike when verse-line lengths vary only slightly. Indent according to rhymes and line lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules for centering and indenting verse material to achieve balanced appearance.
